source: Gutierrez et al. (2025) From RAG to Memory: Non-Parametric Continual Learning for LLMs (HippoRAG 2), ablation
finding: Ablation of how the graph is seeded and built. Matching the whole query to triples (then filtering) beats matching extracted entities (NER to node), which beats matching the query to nodes directly. Dropping passage nodes hurts a lot. The gap 7 pair in the critique (87.1 vs 74.6) is mislabelled: 87.1 is the full query-to-triple design, 74.6 is NER-to-node, and query-to-node is 59.6.
numbers: Passage recall@5 (MuSiQue/2Wiki/HotpotQA/avg): full HippoRAG 2 74.7/90.4/96.3/87.1; NER to node 53.8/91.2/78.8/74.6; query to node 44.9/65.5/68.3/59.6; w/o passage node 63.7/90.3/88.9/81.0; w/o triple filter 73.0/90.7/95.4/86.4. Text: query-to-triple gains 12.5 points recall@5 over NER-to-node. NV-Embed-v2 retriever.
limits: Read from non-layout pdftotext so the columns are reliable. One setup, authors' own runs. Seeds are triples built by an LLM from the query, not free-form thoughts.
agent_relevance: For free-form agent queries, seed the graph by matching the whole thought to stored fact-triples (or to passages), not by extracting entities or matching to bare nodes. Always include passage-level nodes as seeds. Closes gap 7 in direction; the number correction goes to claims.

source: Gutierrez et al. (2025) From RAG to Memory: Non-Parametric Continual Learning for LLMs (HippoRAG 2), QA results
finding: The spread-based memory beats the strongest dense retriever on multi-hop and associative sets and does not lose on simple QA, unlike the first HippoRAG and the other graph methods, which fell below dense retrieval on simple QA.
numbers: F1 with Llama-3.3-70B reader: +9.5 on 2Wiki and +3.1 on LV-Eval over NV-Embed-v2; average about +7 points on associativity tasks (abstract). Robust across dense retrievers, MuSiQue recall@5 dense to HippoRAG 2: GTE-Qwen2-7B 63.6 to 68.8, GritLM-7B 66.0 to 71.6, NV-Embed-v2 69.7 to 74.7. Bootstrap test p<0.05 marked in the table.
limits: Authors' own comparison. The F1 table came out scrambled in extraction, so only figures stated in the text are used. On NQ the gap to dense is small.
agent_relevance: The graph adds roughly 5 recall points on top of any dense retriever on multi-hop. A dense channel stays necessary for simple lookups; keep it as the base channel and add spread on top (gaps 1 and 2).

source: Gutierrez et al. (2025) From RAG to Memory: Non-Parametric Continual Learning for LLMs (HippoRAG 2), corpus growth and graph size
finding: Tested whether the gain survives a growing memory. NQ and MuSiQue were split in four parts (about 250 questions each) and the rest added step by step. HippoRAG 2 stayed ahead of NV-Embed-v2 on both simple and associative questions, but associative performance fell at a similar rate for both as knowledge grew.
numbers: Largest graphs in Table 10 (Llama-3.3-70B OpenIE): about 314k total nodes and 2.67M extracted edges on LV-Eval; 125,777 nodes and 899k extracted edges on NQ. Four-segment growth, F1 plotted in Figure 3.
limits: Scale tested is tens to hundreds of thousands of nodes, not millions. Table 10 columns were scrambled by pdftotext, so node and edge counts are approximate reads. The gap stayed constant, it did not widen.
agent_relevance: Partial answer to gap 6: the margin holds as memory grows 4x at this scale, but absolute multi-hop accuracy still decays. Plan for pruning; do not assume spread cancels growth.

source: Gutierrez et al. (2025) From RAG to Memory: Non-Parametric Continual Learning for LLMs (HippoRAG 2), error analysis
finding: Where HippoRAG 2 fails. Of 100 failures (recall@5 below 1.0), the split was 26% 2-hop, 41% 3-hop, 33% 4-hop. The main sources are the triple filter and the graph search. The filter sometimes throws away the only relevant phrases.
numbers: 7% of samples: no gold phrase matched after query-to-triple, before filtering. 26%: no gold phrase matched after filtering. 8%: filtering lowered the share of matching phrases.
limits: Hand analysis of 100 failures from the authors' own runs. Errors counted among failures only.
agent_relevance: Seeding errors, not the spreading step, dominate misses. The agent should log seed-hit rate and fall back to dense retrieval when seeding returns nothing (gaps 6 and 7).

source: Han et al. (2026, v3) RAG vs. GraphRAG: A Systematic Evaluation and Key Insights, main QA table
finding: A unified benchmark (same preprocessing, retrieval budget, generator Llama-3.1-8B) shows no overall winner. Dense RAG wins on single-hop NQ and detail questions; graph methods win on multi-hop. HippoRAG 2 is best on HotpotQA and MultiHop-RAG but not on NQ.
numbers: NQ F1: RAG 64.78, HippoRAG2 61.03, Community-GraphRAG(Local) 63.01. HotpotQA F1: RAG 60.04, HippoRAG2 63.01, Local 61.66. MultiHop-RAG overall accuracy: RAG 67.02, HippoRAG2 70.27, Local 69.01, RaptorRAG 68.78. Per type: Comparison RAG 92.16 vs HippoRAG2 91.54; Temporal RAG 30.70 vs HippoRAG2 49.91. With reranking or IRCoT, RAG stays better on NQ and graph methods gain more on multi-hop.
limits: Independent group (not the HippoRAG authors), 8B reader. Multi-hop margins are about 3 points, much smaller than the authors' own reports. Single runs.
agent_relevance: Independent evidence for gap 2: the break-even is single-hop fact lookup (NQ: dense +3.8 F1 over HippoRAG 2). The multi-hop gain is real but small (+3.0 HotpotQA, +3.3 MultiHop-RAG).

source: Han et al. (2026, v3) RAG vs. GraphRAG: A Systematic Evaluation and Key Insights, selection and integration
finding: A prompted classifier that sends fact-based queries to dense RAG and reasoning queries to GraphRAG (Selection), and a simple concatenation of both contexts (Integration), both beat the best single method. The two methods fail on different questions.
numbers: Confusion matrix on MultiHop-RAG (Llama-3.1-8B): both right 55.4%, RAG-only 11.6%, GraphRAG-only 13.6%, both wrong 19.4%. HotpotQA: GraphRAG-only 9.8% vs RAG-only 9.2%. NQ: RAG-only 7.8%, GraphRAG-only 6.0%. On MultiHop-RAG with Llama-3.1-70B, Selection and Integration beat the best baseline (exact gains in Figure 3, not extracted). Only about 65.8% (HotpotQA) and 65.5% (NQ) of answer entities appear in the built graph.
limits: The router is an in-context LLM classifier, so its own cost and accuracy are not isolated. Gain sizes are from a figure that was not fully extracted.
agent_relevance: Answers gap 2: yes, a cheap query-type router helps, and running both channels and merging also helps. The 34% of answer entities missing from the extracted graph is direct evidence for gap 6 (extraction noise caps recall).

source: Han et al. (2026, v3) RAG vs. GraphRAG: A Systematic Evaluation and Key Insights, edge and content comparison
finding: A graph made of triples only (relations without the source text) is much worse than dense retrieval; adding source text back recovers part of the loss. LLM-extracted relations alone are a poor memory edge.
numbers: NQ F1: KG-GraphRAG triples only 34.28; triples plus text 50.27; dense RAG 64.78. HotpotQA F1: 25.02; 42.60; dense 60.04. MultiHop-RAG accuracy: 41.24; 48.51; dense 67.02. Community-based Local search (entity-text links) 63.01 NQ / 61.66 HotpotQA.
limits: Comparison of GraphRAG variants, not a clean edge-type ablation. The systems differ in more than edge type.
agent_relevance: Evidence for gap 4: LLM-extracted relations should link back to the raw passages. Treat graph edges as routes to text, not as the memory itself.

source: Xiang et al. (2026) When to use Graphs in RAG: A comprehensive analysis for GraphRAG (GraphRAG-Bench, ICLR 2026), task levels
finding: A benchmark with four task levels (fact retrieval, complex reasoning, summarisation, creative generation) on a novel corpus and a medical corpus. Dense RAG matches or beats graph methods on simple fact retrieval; graph methods win as tasks need more connected concepts. Graph retrieval brings redundant context on simple questions.
numbers: Dense RAG evidence recall on novel-corpus Level 1: 83.2%. On Levels 2-3, HippoRAG evidence recall 87.9-90.9% and HippoRAG2 context relevance 85.8-87.8%. Creative tasks: Global-GraphRAG evidence recall 83.1%, dense context relevance 78.8%. Faithfulness: RAPTOR 70.9%. GPT-4o-mini generator.
limits: Per-cell accuracy tables were scrambled in extraction; only values stated in the text are used. Single benchmark, authors' own.
agent_relevance: A second independent line for gap 2: the break-even is simple fact retrieval. The number of connected facts a question needs is the variable to route on.

source: Xiang et al. (2026) When to use Graphs in RAG: A comprehensive analysis for GraphRAG (GraphRAG-Bench, ICLR 2026), token cost
finding: Prompt length per query differs by orders of magnitude between graph methods. HippoRAG 2 (PPR spreading to passages) keeps the prompt about the same size as dense RAG, so its gains are at roughly equal tokens. Summary-based graph methods use 40x to 400x more.
numbers: Average tokens, novel / medical: dense 879 / 954; HippoRAG2 1008 / 1020; MS-GraphRAG local 38,707 / 39,821; MS-GraphRAG global 331,375 / 332,881; LightRAG about 100,832 / 100,310; Fast-GraphRAG 4,204 / 4,298; RAPTOR 3,441 / 3,510; HippoRAG 7,208 / 7,342.
limits: Prompt tokens at answer time only, not index-building cost. Does not compare against a dense retriever plus one query rewrite.
agent_relevance: Partly answers gap 1 on the token side: spread over a passage-linked graph costs near-equal tokens to dense. The rewrite-versus-spread comparison itself was not found in any source.

source: Dong et al. (2026) Use Graph When It Needs: Efficiently and Adaptively Integrating RAG with Graphs (EA-GraphRAG)
finding: A small MLP router on syntactic features of the query predicts whether GraphRAG will beat dense RAG. It sends easy queries to dense, hard ones to graph retrieval, and fuses both for borderline queries. It beats both pure paths on a mixed benchmark and cuts latency.
numbers: Mixed benchmark accuracy: no retrieval 39.5, dense retrieval 65.1, EA-GraphRAG 71.6 (GPT-Acc 43.4 to 76.9). 2Wiki accuracy vs ColBERTv2: 56.4 to 76.3. Recall on mixed: R@3 66.0, R@5 74.9, +0.4/+0.8 over HippoRAG2 and +8.6/+10.0 over ColBERTv2. Latency per query: dense 0.08 s, graph 3.23 s, router without fusion 1.14 s, router with fusion 2.19 s. Cites prior reports that GraphRAG is 13.4% lower on NQ and 16.6% lower on time-sensitive queries.
limits: Preprint, authors' implementation, GPT-4o-mini reader. The router needs labelled data (queries labelled by whether graph beat dense). Features are syntactic and may not transfer to free-form agent thoughts.
agent_relevance: Answers the second half of gap 2: yes, a cheap router can predict when graph spread pays off. A first rule for us: spread only if the thought names two or more entities or asks for a relation.

source: Fu et al. (2026) GraphRAG-Router: Learning Cost-Efficient Routing over GraphRAGs and LLMs with RL (abstract and introduction read)
finding: Different QA sets prefer different graph retrievers (entity lookup prefers local subgraph search, thematic questions prefer community summaries). A router trained by supervised warm-up and two-stage RL picks the retriever and the generator size and cuts overuse of the large LLM by nearly 30%.
numbers: Six general and multi-hop QA benchmarks; about 30% fewer large-model calls (abstract). Per-benchmark scores not extracted.
limits: Only the abstract and introduction were read; result tables were not checked. The RL router needs training data.
agent_relevance: Supports routing by question type as a design pattern. Do not copy the RL training; a rule-based router is enough as a first version.

source: HeLa-Mem authors (2026) HeLa-Mem: Hebbian Learning and Associative Memory for LLM Agents
finding: An agent memory whose edges are learned by co-activation (edges between memories retrieved together get stronger and decay), with spreading activation as a second retrieval path next to semantic search. Switching off spreading activation costs 2.6 F1 on LoCoMo; the reflective consolidation agent matters more.
numbers: LoCoMo, GPT-4o-mini, average F1: full 34.74; without spreading activation 32.19 (multi-hop 36.04 to 33.88, temporal 46.23 to 44.36, open 29.50 to 27.76, single 45.04 to 43.34); without reflective agent 29.87; without forgetting 34.28 (no loss, conversations only 300 turns). Parameters: edge decay 0.995, spreading strength 0.1, threshold 0.6, learning rate 0.02. About 1,010 tokens per query. Main-text multi-hop F1 40.14 (MemoryOS 38.39, A-Mem 27.02).
limits: Single lab. The ablation table multi-hop value (36.04) differs from the main-text value (40.14), so the two come from different runs. Baseline numbers are copied from other papers. Edges are learned by co-activation, not extracted by an LLM.
agent_relevance: Evidence for gap 4: co-activation (usage-learned) edges are a third edge type that works. Spread adds about 2.5 F1 here, versus 5.4 F1 for the fan effect in SYNAPSE; effect sizes are modest and come from different setups.

finding: On a second benchmark (LongMemEval-S, 500 items, GPT-4o-mini judge) the associative memory wins overall and on temporal, multi-session and knowledge-update questions, but loses on the single-session (simple fact) type to plain dense retrieval.
numbers: Overall accuracy: HeLa-Mem 65.40, A-MEM 62.60, NaiveRAG 61.00, FullText 56.80, Mem0 53.61. Single type: NaiveRAG 85.90, A-MEM 84.62, HeLa-Mem 78.85, FullText 78.21. Temporal: HeLa 50.38 vs NaiveRAG 39.85. Multi-session: 57.14 vs 48.48. Knowledge update: 78.21 vs 67.95.
limits: Single lab; some baseline numbers copied. The single type is a small slice, so the 7-point deficit has a wide error band (no confidence interval given).
agent_relevance: A third observation of the same break-even (gap 2): associative spread helps on questions that link sessions and loses to plain dense retrieval on one-fact lookups.

source: SuperLocalMemory V3.3 authors (2026) The Living Brain (SYNAPSE-style spreading activation in a 7-channel retriever)
finding: A second code base re-implements the SYNAPSE spreading-activation formulation as one of seven retrieval channels. Results are mixed: gains on multi-hop and adversarial, a loss on single-hop, and a lower total than the authors' previous 4-channel version. It does not isolate the spread channel, so it is not a clean replication of SYNAPSE.
numbers: LoCoMo, 2 of 10 conversations, 304 QA pairs, zero-LLM retrieval mode: V3.3 70.4% overall (214/304) vs 74.8% for the previous version. Versus its own retrieval baseline (62.8%): multi-hop 25.4 to 49.2 (+23.8 points), temporal +15.3, adversarial +12.7, single-hop 60.5 to 65.1 (+4.6), open-domain 86.8 to 82.5 (-4.3). Single-hop is 14.9 points below the previous version. Judge: GPT-5.4-mini.
limits: Small sample (304 questions, 2 conversations). The authors credit the gains to cross-channel intersection and session diversity, not to spread alone. One author group; independence from the SYNAPSE authors is not established.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 stays open: there is no isolated, independent re-test of SYNAPSE. This adds a second data point that more channels cost simple queries, and the authors suggest query-dependent routing, which fits d10.

source: Park, Cho, Lee (2025) Stop-RAG: Value-Based Retrieval Control for Iterative RAG
finding: A learned stop controller (Q-network on DeBERTa-v3-large, trained on full trajectories) beats both a fixed number of iterations and a prompted stop check on two of three multi-hop sets. Prompting the model to stop is about as good as no stopping.
numbers: Own pipeline (Llama-3.1-8B, Contriever, up to 10 iterations), EM/F1/Acc for raw vs LLM-Stop vs Stop-RAG: MuSiQue 34.5/44.8/41.1, 34.2/44.6/41.3, 36.8/47.0/43.9; 2Wiki 64.9/73.1/65.9, 64.9/73.3/66.1, 68.2/75.7/69.0; HotpotQA 51.0/65.0/60.8, 51.4/65.2/60.7, 52.4/66.1/62.6. On CoRAG, HotpotQA is slightly worse with Stop-RAG (F1 67.5 raw vs 67.4). 1,000 test questions per set.
limits: Iterative RAG with a query-generating LLM, not spreading activation over a graph. Needs training data and a trained model; gains are 1 to 3 F1 points.
agent_relevance: Gap 10: a learned stop exists and gains 1-3 F1 over fixed depth, but the gain is modest and needs training. For us a simple evidence-coverage rule (d17) is the cheaper first step.

source: Li et al. (2026, v3) TreeHop: Efficient Embedding-Level Query Rewriter
finding: Multi-hop retrieval by updating the query embedding after each retrieved chunk (no LLM rewrite, no graph), with a rule-based stop that prunes redundant branches. It is the closest published 'dense plus iterative rewrite' alternative to graph spread, and it is cheap.
numbers: Four MHQA sets (HotpotQA 7,405; 2Wiki 9,536; MuSiQue 2,417; MultiHop-RAG 816 queries). Latency about 0.1 s per query at iteration 2 and 0.2 s at iteration 3; 92.8%-97.8% lower than LLM-based iterative methods. Uses 2.2%-29.4% of competitors' parameters. Direct retrieval completes the full evidence chain for only 12.7%-43.5% of queries; by iteration 3 TreeHop adds 11.3-35.4 points of chain recall. On MuSiQue recall is 0.4% below Iter-RetGen.
limits: Retrieval recall only; not compared with HippoRAG, SYNAPSE or any spreading-activation method. Needs a trained 0.18B model.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 stays open: the strongest rewrite baseline found was never run head to head against graph spread. It is the baseline to include when we build our own test.

source: Roh and Han (2026) HALT: Verification-Aware Stopping for Retrieval-Augmented Search Agents
finding: Stop when the gathered evidence covers each expected hop claim, not when the generator is confident. Needs no retraining of the search agent. With claims generated from the question, savings are smaller but exact match is preserved; with gold claims savings are larger.
numbers: Self-Ask agents 3B and 7B on HotpotQA, 2Wiki, MuSiQue (1,000 questions each). The 3B agent runs to its search budget instead of stopping on its own for 87.5% / 78.1% / 81.2% of questions. Gold-claim diagnostic: loop reductions up to 37% / 45% / 20% (table). On the under-covered HotpotQA subset (n=511), forcing continuation to coverage lifts EM from 0.162 to 0.323 (+16.0 points). A prompted sufficiency judge fires on 43% of questions, too early.
limits: Search-agent loops, not spreading activation. Deployable gains (generated claims) are smaller than the gold-claim figures. One independent-researcher preprint.
agent_relevance: Gap 10: the fixed depth T=3 is a reasonable default, and an evidence-coverage stop (does the context hold each needed claim?) is a better training-free stop than a confidence prompt. Agents both over-search and under-search.

source: Abramski, Rossetti, Stella (2025) A word association network methodology for evaluating implicit biases in LLMs compared to humans
finding: Builds association networks from LLM-generated free associations (Mistral, Llama3, Haiku) and from humans (SWOW), runs spreading activation from prime words, and compares the final activation of stereotype-consistent vs inconsistent targets. This gives a repeatable audit for bias in an association graph.
numbers: Gender stereotypes: significant positive effects (paired Wilcoxon) in all four networks; humans strongest, Mistral weakest; female stereotypes stronger than male in Mistral and Haiku, the reverse in Llama3. Valence and emotion probes for religion, ethnicity, sexual orientation and politics. LLM networks showed counter-biases not seen in humans (Mistral and Llama3 rated muslim more positive than christian). All three models associated african with lower valence.
limits: The network is built from LLM free association, not from the retrieval store an agent would use. No retrieval task was run, so it shows the networks carry stereotypes, not that retrieval outputs shift. Effect-size values are in a figure, not extracted.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: a ready audit recipe. Build the agent's own memory graph, seed with demographic prime words, spread, and compare activation of stereotyped vs non-stereotyped targets before and after any retrieval policy change. The 2026 follow-up named in the critique was not located.

source: Abramski et al. (2024) The LLM World of Words English free association norms generated by large language models
finding: The first large LLM free-association norms, built with the same cues as human SWOW (12,282 cues; 100 sets of 3 responses per cue). LLM-built networks differ from the human one: two of the three LLMs use a much narrower vocabulary, so their graphs have fewer distinct nodes.
numbers: After cleaning (11,545 cues): unique responses humans 116,640; Llama3 105,367; Mistral 41,369; Haiku 15,275. Total responses about 3.1-3.4 million per network. Missing responses: humans 9.1%, Mistral 5.6%, Llama3 3.3%, Haiku 1.7%.
limits: Data descriptor; no retrieval test. Vocabulary size depends on the authors' prompt and sampling settings.
agent_relevance: Gaps 9 and 4: an LLM-built association graph is a narrow, hub-heavy version of the human one, so it may amplify frequent associations. Prefer edges tied to stored text over LLM-invented associations, and audit with d18.
